cards.title: Zed/tree-sitter grammar is a stale dialect — fix broken highlighting
cards.body: The Zed extension highlights an OLD dialect, so keywords light up inside identifiers (format->for, inner->in, asset->as, reference->ref, mutable->mut, usage->use, tests->test). Two multiplicative root causes. (1) grammar.js has NO `word: $ => $.identifier` token, so tree-sitter does no keyword extraction and keyword tokens match as PREFIXES of identifiers, worst in the ERROR/partial states that dominate live editing. (2) the grammar still defines retired constructs (val/var bindings, switch_stmt) and CANNOT parse modern ratified syntax real examples use (@=/:= sigil bindings, multi-arm `if subj == { pat -> {} }`, enum/or/range/wildcard patterns, ~^&* capability sigils, fan-out f.[…]/s.{…}, ??, dotted `use core.x.y`, map literals, self/~self, #Unsafe/#Uninit/#-attributes, block comments /* */) and REQUIRES `;` terminators modern Jet omits — so nearly every file is full of ERROR nodes, compounding (1). highlights/outline/indents.scm still tag retired switch/val/var. No new user-facing syntax — the grammar just needs to track already-ratified syntax, so NO ballot. Authoritative source: editors/tree-sitter/grammar.js; ship via FORCE=1 editors/zed/install.sh (regen parser.c + wasm + re-pin extension.toml), update the four .scm/config.toml query files in lockstep (a dangling node ref is a hard Zed load failure). Plan: tools/Tower/docs/sidequests/zed-grammar-modernization.md.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in tools/Tower/docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

questions.text: I'm leaning towards A, but how is bloat/buildup addressed? For large codebases, how will users be able to avoid 3k lines of code that are just migrations?
questions.answer: Bloat is bounded by published-API surface × support window, NOT codebase size, via four bounds: (1) only `#PublishedSchema` types accrue migrations — internal types never do; (2) migrations live in `migrations/`, are build-tier, and cost zero at runtime; (3) you keep migrations only back to your declared support floor; (4) `jet schema squash` collapses old chains into a fresh baseline snapshot. So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?
questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: For generics, we use <T> -> can we use that?
questions.answer: Two things were colliding on the brackets. `[Particle]` is Jet's *list type* ("a list of Particle"), NOT a generic parameter — generics stay `<T>` and are untouched by this card. The old gist's `columnar [T]` just meant "the keyword in front of a list type," where T was the element. So the real question is the *spelling* of the per-container form, and yes — a generic-style `Columnar<Particle>` is now a real option (B) alongside the prefix keyword `columnar [Particle]` (A). The difference: A reads as a storage modifier on the same list type (no new type, same API, just a layout hint), while B (`<T>`-style) makes layout part of the type identity — `Columnar<Particle>` becomes a distinct container needing conversions and its own impls/trait bounds, like `Map<K,V>`. Recommendation stays A: a layout is how a value is *stored*, not a type parameter, and the prefix keyword keeps one word (`columnar`) across both the struct attribute and the per-use form. `<T>`-style is available as B if you'd rather layout live in the type system. questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.
